title: Why did the industry move beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows (thread blocking, thread-pool exhaustion, HTTP 202 Accepted, accept-then-process), and what does async communication actually improve?
shortTitle: Why did the industry move beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows

s1_definition.profdef: Synchronous REST holds a request thread open until the work finishes and the response is returned. For long-running workflows this blocks a thread for the entire duration, and under load the fixed-size server thread pool is exhausted, so new requests queue or are rejected even though the machine is not CPU-bound. The industry moved to an accept-then-process model where the server validates the request, enqueues the work, immediately returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a tracking handle, and processes asynchronously, which decouples request acceptance from work completion.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks the bank teller to process a complex international transfer that takes ten minutes of back-office checks. In the synchronous model the teller stands frozen at the counter for ten minutes doing nothing but waiting, and the queue behind Rajesh grows until the whole branch jams. In the asynchronous model the teller takes the form, hands Rajesh a token number, says "we will notify you", and immediately serves the next customer while the back office does the slow work. The counter never freezes.
s1_definition.oneliner: Synchronous REST ties up a thread for the entire job and exhausts the pool under load, so for long work we accept-then-process, return 202 with a handle, and finish asynchronously.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Synchronous REST holds a request thread open until the work finishes and the response is returned. For long-running workflows this blocks a thread for the entire duration, and under load the fixed-size server thread pool is exhausted, so new requests queue or are rejected even though the machine is not CPU-bound. The industry moved to an accept-then-process model where the server validates the request, enqueues the work, immediately returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a tracking handle, and processes asynchronously, which decouples request acceptance from work completion.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh asks the bank teller to process a complex international transfer that takes ten minutes of back-office checks. In the synchronous model the teller stands frozen at the counter for ten minutes doing nothing but waiting, and the queue behind Rajesh grows until the whole branch jams. In the asynchronous model the teller takes the form, hands Rajesh a token number, says "we will notify you", and immediately serves the next customer while the back office does the slow work. The counter never freezes.

**One line to remember:** Synchronous REST ties up a thread for the entire job and exhausts the pool under load, so for long work we accept-then-process, return 202 with a handle, and finish asynchronously.

sections.s2_technical:
A server has a bounded thread pool, for example Tomcat defaults to around two hundred worker threads. In synchronous REST, one request occupies one thread from the moment it arrives until the response is written. If a workflow takes ten seconds, that thread is unavailable for ten seconds. The critical insight is that this thread is mostly idle, blocked waiting on a slow downstream call or a long computation, not doing useful CPU work. So you can exhaust all two hundred threads while the CPU sits at five percent utilization. Once the pool is exhausted, new requests wait in the accept queue and eventually time out or get rejected, and the whole service appears down even though it is not overloaded in any real sense. This is thread-pool exhaustion, and it is the core reason synchronous REST fails for long-running workflows.

The accept-then-process pattern breaks the coupling between accepting a request and completing its work. The endpoint does only the fast part synchronously: validate the input, persist a record of the requested work with a status of PENDING, enqueue a message or schedule the job, and return immediately. The correct HTTP response is 202 Accepted, which literally means "I have accepted your request for processing but have not completed it". The response includes a handle, typically a resource URL like `/transfers/TXF-123/status` or a job id, so the client can poll for progress or receive a callback or webhook when the work finishes. The request thread is released in milliseconds and is immediately available for the next request.

What does asynchronous communication actually improve? First, throughput and resilience under load: because threads are released quickly, a small pool can accept a huge number of requests, and a burst of long-running work no longer jams the front door. Second, decoupling: the acceptance path and the processing path can scale independently, so you can add more background workers without touching the API layer. Third, failure isolation and retries: a failed job can be retried from the queue without the client having to resend, and a slow downstream service only backs up the worker pool, not the public API. Fourth, better user experience for genuinely long work: the client gets immediate acknowledgment and a way to track progress instead of staring at a spinner that may time out at the HTTP layer anyway.

There are senior nuances. Asynchronous processing introduces the need for idempotency, because the client may retry the accept call and must not create duplicate work, so you use an idempotency key. It introduces the need for status tracking and notification, since the client no longer gets the result inline. And it shifts complexity from a simple blocking call to a workflow with states, which is why long multi-step workflows often graduate to a Saga or a workflow engine. It is also worth distinguishing this from reactive or non-blocking REST: reactive frameworks free the thread during I/O waits and help with throughput, but they do not by themselves solve the semantics of genuinely long-running, multi-minute workflows, where accept-then-process with a durable job record is still the right model.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's international transfer involves fraud screening, correspondent-bank checks, and SWIFT messaging that together take several seconds to minutes, and the synchronous endpoint held a thread the whole time. During a morning spike the two-hundred-thread pool filled with transfers waiting on SWIFT, and simple balance-check requests started failing. This is exactly the thread-pool exhaustion problem that pushed us off synchronous REST.

Problem 2 — Customers watched a spinner for a minute and often the browser or gateway timed out before SWIFT replied, so they resubmitted, creating duplicate transfers. This is exactly what accept-then-process with 202 and an idempotency key fixes.

Problem 3 — The operations team could not retry a transfer that failed on a transient correspondent-bank error without the customer resending. This is exactly what a durable job record plus a background worker enables, because the worker can retry from the persisted PENDING job.

Our mini-project builds an international transfer service in the accept-then-process style. The code defines a `TransferRequest`, a `TransferJob` with a status lifecycle, a `TransferController` that validates, persists a PENDING job, enqueues it, and returns 202 with a status URL, a `TransferWorker` that processes jobs from the queue asynchronously and updates status, and a demo that submits a transfer, shows the immediate 202, then shows the background completion and the polled final status.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: international transfer of 50000 from SAV2001 to an IBAN, with idempotency key idem-rajesh-001.

Step 1: The controller validates the amount, then persists a `TransferJob` with status PENDING keyed by the idempotency key. If the same key arrived again it would return the existing job rather than create a duplicate.

Step 2: The controller enqueues the job id and immediately returns a 202 Accepted carrying the job id and a status URL. The request thread is released in milliseconds, ready for the next caller.

Step 3: The background worker, running on its own thread, polls the queue, picks up the job, and sets its status to PROCESSING. The slow SWIFT and fraud work happens here, off the request thread.

Step 4: While the worker runs, the client polls the status URL and sees PENDING then PROCESSING. The public API stayed responsive throughout.

Step 5: The worker finishes the slow work and sets the job status to COMPLETED. The next poll returns COMPLETED, and the client knows the transfer is done without ever having held a connection open for the full duration.

```
2026-10-24 14:09:50 INFO    ACCEPTED job TXF-1a2b3c4d (PENDING), returning 202
2026-10-24 14:09:50 INFO    CLIENT got 202 Accepted, track at /api/v1/transfers/TXF-1a2b3c4d/status
2026-10-24 14:09:50 INFO    WORKER processing TXF-1a2b3c4d (SWIFT + fraud checks)
2026-10-24 14:09:50 INFO    CLIENT polled status = PROCESSING
2026-10-24 14:09:51 INFO    WORKER completed TXF-1a2b3c4d
2026-10-24 14:09:51 INFO    CLIENT polled status = COMPLETED
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: POST /api/v1/transfers {from:SAV2001, to:IBAN, amount:50000, idem:idem-rajesh-001}
    │
    ▼
  TransferController (FAST accept path — thread held for ~1ms)
    │ validate amount>0
    │ JobStore.saveNewOrExisting → TXF-1a2b (PENDING)   (idempotent)
    │ queue.offer(TXF-1a2b)
    │
    ├──────────────▶ 202 Accepted {jobId, statusUrl}   ◀── thread RELEASED
    │
    ▼ (queue)
  TransferWorker (SLOW path — separate thread pool)
    │ poll → TXF-1a2b → status PROCESSING
    │ SWIFT + fraud checks (700ms)  ← would have blocked a request thread
    │ status COMPLETED
    ▼
  JobStore: TXF-1a2b = COMPLETED
    ▲
  Client polls GET /transfers/TXF-1a2b/status ─┘ PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED

  ── Sync vs Async thread usage ──
  SYNC : 1 request = 1 thread held 700ms → 200 threads exhausted fast
  ASYNC: 1 request = 1 thread held 1ms   → pool stays free, workers do slow work
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The industry moved beyond synchronous REST for long-running workflows because of a specific, measurable failure mode called thread-pool exhaustion. A server has a bounded pool of worker threads, and in synchronous REST one request occupies one thread from arrival until the response is written. For a workflow that takes seconds or minutes, that thread is held the whole time, and the crucial point is that it is mostly idle, blocked waiting on a slow downstream, not doing CPU work. So you can exhaust all your threads while the CPU is nearly idle, and new requests queue and time out even though the machine is not truly overloaded.

The fix is the accept-then-process pattern, which breaks the coupling between accepting a request and completing its work. The endpoint does only the fast part synchronously: it validates the input, persists a durable record of the requested work with a PENDING status, enqueues the job, and immediately returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a handle such as a status URL. The 202 status literally means the request has been accepted for processing but is not complete, and the handle lets the client poll or receive a callback. The request thread is released in milliseconds, so a small pool can accept a huge volume of work and a burst of slow jobs no longer jams the front door.

What asynchronous communication actually improves is fourfold. It improves throughput and resilience under load because threads are freed quickly. It improves decoupling because the accept path and the processing path scale independently, so I can add background workers without touching the API. It improves failure handling because a failed job is retried from the queue without the client resending, and a slow downstream only backs up the workers, not the public API. And it improves user experience for genuinely long work because the client gets an immediate acknowledgment and a way to track progress instead of staring at a spinner that the HTTP layer may time out anyway.

On my project at National Bank of India the international transfer involved fraud screening, correspondent-bank checks, and SWIFT messaging that together took seconds to minutes. The synchronous endpoint held a thread for the whole duration, and during a morning spike the pool filled with transfers waiting on SWIFT while simple balance checks started failing, and customers whose browsers timed out resubmitted and created duplicate transfers. We rebuilt it as accept-then-process: validate, persist a PENDING job with an idempotency key, enqueue, return 202 with a status URL, and let a pool of background workers do the slow SWIFT work and retry transient failures. The API stayed fast, duplicates disappeared because of the idempotency key, and operations could retry failed jobs from the durable record.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that synchronous REST holds a thread for the entire job and exhausts the pool under long-running load even while the CPU is idle, so for long work I accept-then-process, return 202 with a tracking handle, and complete asynchronously, which gives me throughput, decoupling, retryable failure handling, and a responsive API.
